content: The typhoid vaccine is available in two forms in the United States: an oral live attenuated vaccine (Vivotif Berna, derived from the Ty21a strain of Salmonella Typhi and manufactured by the Swiss Serum and Vaccine Institute) and an intramuscular Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (ViCPS, marketed as Typhim Vi by Sanofi Pasteur). Both vaccines provide protection to approximately 50% to 80% of recipients. The intramuscular heat-phenol-inactivated vaccine, previously manufactured by Wyeth-Ayerst, was discontinued in 2000. Combined hepatitis A/typhoid fever vaccines are not licensed in the United States but may be available in other countries. The time required for primary vaccination and the minimum age for administration differ between the two vaccines. For the oral Ty21a vaccine, primary vaccination involves taking four capsules, one every other day. These capsules must be refrigerated (but not frozen) and taken approximately one hour before a meal with cool or lukewarm water (not exceeding 37°C or 98.6°F). All four doses must be completed to achieve maximum efficacy, and the regimen should be finished at least one week before potential exposure. This vaccine is not recommended for infants or children under six years of age. The ViCPS vaccine is administered as a single 0.5 mL (25 µg) intramuscular dose. It should be given at least two weeks before potential exposure to allow the vaccine to take effect. The manufacturer does not recommend this vaccine for infants or children under two years of age. Adverse Reactions Information on adverse reactions is limited. There is no available data on the safety of these vaccines during pregnancy, and it is generally advised to avoid vaccinating pregnant women on theoretical grounds. The live attenuated Ty21a vaccine should not be administered to immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV infection. For this group, the intramuscular ViCPS vaccine is considered a safer alternative. The only contraindication to the ViCPS vaccine is a history of severe local or systemic reactions to a previous dose. Neither vaccine should be administered to individuals with an acute febrile illness. Precautions and Contraindications The immunogenicity of the live attenuated Ty21a vaccine may theoretically be reduced in individuals concurrently receiving antibiotics, immune globulin, or viral vaccines. The growth of the live Ty21a strain is inhibited in vitro by various antibacterial agents. Vaccination with Ty21a should be delayed for more than 24 hours after the administration of any antibacterial agent. However, available data do not suggest that simultaneous administration of oral polio or yellow fever vaccines reduces the immunogenicity of Ty21a. If typhoid vaccination is warranted, it should not be delayed due to the administration of viral vaccines. Simultaneous administration of Ty21a and immune globulin does not appear to pose a problem. What You Need to Know 1. What is typhoid? Typhoid fever is a serious illness caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi. It can lead to high fever, weakness, stomach pain, headache, loss of appetite, and sometimes a rash. If untreated, it can be fatal in up to 30% of cases. Some individuals who recover from typhoid become carriers, capable of spreading the disease to others. Typhoid is typically contracted through contaminated food or water. In the United States, most cases occur in individuals who have traveled abroad. Globally, typhoid affects approximately 21 million people annually and causes around 200,000 deaths. Vaccination can help prevent typhoid. 2. Typhoid Vaccines There are two vaccines available to prevent typhoid: An inactivated (killed) vaccine administered as an injection. A live attenuated (weakened) vaccine taken orally. 3. Who Should Get the Typhoid Vaccine and When? Routine typhoid vaccination is not recommended in the United States. However, it is advised for: Travelers to regions where typhoid is common. (Note: The vaccine is not 100% effective and does not replace careful attention to food and water safety.) Individuals in close contact with a typhoid carrier. Laboratory workers handling Salmonella Typhi bacteria. Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection): Not recommended for children under two years of age. A single dose provides protection and should be administered at least two weeks before travel. A booster dose is required every two years for individuals at continued risk. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral): Not recommended for children under six years of age. Four doses are required, taken two days apart. The final dose should be completed at least one week before travel. A booster dose is needed every five years for individuals at continued risk. Both vaccines can be administered alongside other vaccines. 4. Who Should Not Get the Typhoid Vaccine or Should Wait? Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection): Individuals who have had a severe reaction to a previous dose should not receive another dose. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral): Individuals who have had a severe reaction to a previous dose should not receive another dose. Those with weakened immune systems should not receive this vaccine and should opt for the inactivated vaccine instead. This includes individuals with: HIV/AIDS or other immune-compromising conditions. Ongoing treatment with immune-suppressing drugs, such as steroids, for two weeks or longer. Cancer or those undergoing cancer treatment with radiation or chemotherapy. The oral vaccine should not be administered within 24 hours of certain antibiotics. Consult a healthcare provider for more information. 5. What Are the Risks of the Typhoid Vaccine? Like any medication, vaccines can potentially cause serious side effects, such as severe allergic reactions. However, the risk of serious harm or death from a vaccine is extremely low. Serious adverse events from either typhoid vaccine are very rare. Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection): Mild reactions may include: Fever (in about 1 in 100 people). Headache (in about 3 in 100 people). Redness or swelling at the injection site (in about 7 in 100 people). Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral): Mild reactions may include: Fever or headache (in about 5 in 100 people). Abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or rash (rare). 6. What If There Is a Moderate or Severe Reaction? What to Look For: Any unusual condition, such as a high fever or behavioral changes. Signs of a severe allergic reaction, including difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. What to Do: Contact a doctor or seek medical attention immediately. Inform the healthcare provider about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Ask the healthcare provider to report the reaction to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by visiting [vaers.hhs.gov](http://vaers.hhs.gov) or calling 1-800-822-7967. 7. How Can I Learn More? Consult your doctor or nurse. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend additional resources. Contact your local or state health department.
